A halibut is a type of fish — specifically, a large, flat fish that lives in cold ocean water.
What kind of fish it is

Halibut belongs to a group called flatfish. As the name suggests, flatfish have bodies that are extremely flat — almost like a thick, wide oval. Other flatfish you may have heard of include flounder and sole. Among all flatfish, halibut is by far the largest.

Imagine taking a regular fish and pressing it completely flat, so it becomes a wide, disc-like shape. That's roughly what a halibut looks like.

One of the most unusual things about halibut — and all flatfish — is the placement of its eyes. Unlike most fish, where one eye is on each side of the head, both of a halibut's eyes are on the same side of its body (the top side). This is because halibut spend their lives lying flat on the ocean floor, so having both eyes on top allows them to look upward and spot prey or danger.

  • The top side (facing up toward the water surface) is dark — usually brownish or grayish-green. This coloring acts as camouflage against the dark ocean floor when viewed from above.
  • The bottom side (facing down, resting on the seafloor) is white or pale.

Halibut can grow to be extremely large. While an average adult halibut weighs around 25–35 kg (55–77 lbs), large individuals can weigh over 200 kg (440 lbs) and measure over 2 meters (about 7 feet) in length. This makes it one of the biggest fish with a bony skeleton in the world.

Halibut are found in the cold waters of the North Atlantic and North Pacific Oceans — places like Alaska, Canada, Norway, and Iceland. They live mostly near the bottom of the ocean, in depths ranging from shallow coastal areas to several hundred meters deep. They prefer cold, clear, well-oxygenated waters.

There are two main kinds:

  • Pacific halibut — found in the North Pacific Ocean
  • Atlantic halibut — found in the North Atlantic Ocean

Both are the same basic type of fish; the Pacific halibut is simply from a different ocean and is the more common of the two.

Halibut are predators. Despite lying on the ocean floor, they are fast and agile swimmers when they need to be. They eat other fish, squid, octopus, crabs, and other sea creatures. They often ambush their prey by lying still on the floor and then lunging upward quickly.

Halibut is one of the most popular and prized seafood choices worldwide. Its flesh is:

  • White and firm — it holds together well when cooked
  • Mild in flavor — not "fishy" tasting, which makes it appealing even to people who don't normally enjoy fish
  • Low in fat — making it a lean source of protein

It is commonly prepared by baking, grilling, pan-frying, or poaching. You'll find it on menus at seafood restaurants and in grocery stores, often sold as fillets or steaks.

The word halibut stays the same whether you're talking about one fish or many. You can say "I caught a halibut" (one fish) or "We caught three halibut" (multiple fish). The form "halibuts" exists but is rarely used.

A halibut is a very large, flat, ocean-floor-dwelling fish with both eyes on one side of its body, found in cold North Atlantic and North Pacific waters. It is a powerful predator underwater and a highly valued food fish on the dinner table.
